newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Daimler-Benz discussing stake hike with Ssangyong.
newsitem.headline: Daimler-Benz discussing stake hike with Ssangyong.

text.p: South Korea's Ssangyong Group and its German partner Daimler-Benz AG said on Thursday they were holding talks on increasing the German firm's stake in cash-starved Ssangyong Motor.
Analysts said the additional capital injection, if realised, would be a great relief to Ssangyong and could give the German firm managerial control of the South Korean automaker.
But some said they were not sure why Daimler-Benz, known for its commitment to sound financial fundamentals, would want to increase its stake in a money-losing firm.

"The German company's aid will be a good solution for Ssangyong Motor because the Korean automaker has a very slim chance of recovering from its financial troubles," said Jee Sung-chul, an analyst at LG Securities.
"In exchange for the new capital, Daimler-Benz will impose its own management style, especially in the fields of marketing," he added.
Officials from the two companies said the results of the negotiations were expected in a month or so.
"We are now discussing the issue with Ssangyong. But the result will, we expect, come out at around the end of August or early in September," said Daimler-Benz spokesman May Dedles.
"We are tapping various business possiblities with Ssangyong because we are interested in what is going on in the fast-growing Asian market," he told Reuters from his office in Germany.
A senior Ssangyong Motor financial manager earlier told Reuters the two companies had tentatively agreed that Daimler-Benz would raise its stake in Ssangyong to 45 percent or more from 2.55 percent.
But spokesmen for the two companies denied any agreements had been reached yet.
Analysts said the sheer size of Ssangyong Motor's debt and its militant labour union would be stumbling blocks to any deal.
"I don't see why Daimler-Benz, which is keen on sound financial footings, is interested in increasing its stake in Ssangyong," said Nam Seung-soo, analyst at Daishin Economic Research Institute.
Ssangyong Motor has suffered from huge losses as result of massive investment in new models, including its "Chairman" luxury sedan that will go on sale from October.
Ssangyong's debts are currently estimated at 3.2 trillion won ($3.58 billion). The specialist four-wheel-drive utility maker posted losses of 228.5 billion won in 1996 on sales of 1.37 trillion won.
South Korea's car sales have suffered this year because of an economic slowdown, and analysts said they did not expect Ssangyong to fare any better this year.
They said one of Ssangyong's biggest weaknesses was is its lack of mass-production lines.
Ssangyong said it had paid-in capital of about 300 billion won. Daimler-Benz's stake would be raised through a capital increase.
Analysts said the Ssangyong Group may ultimately want to sell its automaking unit as its snowballing debts were increasingly weakening the group's financial structure.
"Rumours about financial troubles at Ssangyong Motor began circulating more intensively after the Kia crisis," said an analyst at Dongwon Economic Research Institute.
"Once a group or a company has become caught up in such swirling rumours, chances of recovery are really slim."
